catalog_quote: The accent (stress) in Chaldean is cumulative and has no distinctive function. Its position is completely predictable. In monosyllabic words, it falls on the vocalic element irrespective of other features, and in polysyllabic words it regularly falls on the penultimate. It functions as the principal reliable phonological demarcative feature indicating word boundaries. /béθa/ 'house' /beθóxin/ 'your house'

new_statements.quote: The accent (stress) in Chaldean is cumulative and has no distinctive function. Its position is completely predictable. In monosyllabic words, it falls on the vocalic element irrespective of other features, and in polysyllabic words it regularly falls on the penultimate. It functions as the principal reliable phonological demarcative feature indicating word boundaries. /béθa/ 'house' /beθóxin/ 'your house'
new_statements.citation: Sara, Solomon I. 1974. A Description of Modern Chaldean (Janua Linguarum, Series Practica 213). The Hague/Paris: Mouton.
new_statements.locator: p. 22, ch. 'Phonology', §1.0 'Phonology of the word', a. 'Prosody of the word'
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (Google Books preview page scan of Sara 1974, De Gruyter e-reprint). The page is headed PHONOLOGY / 1.0 PHONOLOGY OF THE word / a. Prosody of the word, and reads word for word: 'The accent (stress) in Chaldean is cumulative and has no distinctive function. Its position is completely predictable. In monosyllabic words, it falls on the vocalic element irrespective of other features, and in polysyllabic words it regularly falls on the penultimate. It functions as the principal reliable phonological demarcative feature indicating word boundaries. /béθa/ 'house' /beθóxin/ 'your house''. The quote is verbatim at the stated locator (p. 22, sec. 1.0a); is the end of the Introduction, confirm…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is non-contrastive and predictable: it falls on the penultimate syllable of any polysyllabic word (and on the only vowel of a monosyllable); suffixation moves it rightward so that it stays penultimate (béθa -> beθóxin).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said about secondary stress in Sara; none of the other sources read describe a secondary-stress rule (Khan 2002 and Napiorkowska 2015 treat phrase-level 'stress groups'/nuclear stress instead).
new_statements.exceptions: Sara states none. Corroborating sources for sister Chaldean/Mosul-Plain varieties list exceptions: Khan 2002 (Qaraqosh, snippets pp. 67-68): pronominal object suffixes on verbs often ignored (k-ódilə), stress shifted to the final syllable in some verb forms (k-amaxwalhá), irregular stress in some loanwords, nuclear stress may move to the final syllable at the end of an intonation group (p. 471); Napiorkowska 2015 (Diyana-Zariwaw, p. 64): initial stress in vocatives (b-ʾálaha), 2pl pronoun ʾaxtū́n final, mádənxa 'East', enclitic copula/possessive suffixes do not count (brátela); Maclean 1895 §8: vocatives initial, 3pl-suffixed words and -a'it adverbs oxytone, 2pl suffix/pl. imperative antepenultimate, enclitics count as part of the word; Rhétoré 1912 §71 (older, divergent): claims final stress in consonant-final words (kthawan, chaklet) and penultimate in vowel-final words, foreign words keep their accent unless nativized.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level rule for citation forms; Sara calls stress the demarcative signal of word boundaries. Khan 2002 ch. 6 and Coghill 2019 n. 7 describe phrase-level 'stress groups' (proclitic/enclitic combinations bearing a single stress, e.g. numeral + noun with stress shifted to the numeral's final syllable) and intonation-group-final shift of nuclear stress to the ultima in lively narrative/Gospel reading (Khan 2002: 471-473).
new_statements.identity_note: Sara 1974 describes 'Modern Chaldean' as spoken in Mangesh (Christian/Chaldean town in Dohuk province near the Turkish border, the author's native dialect), one of the dialects Glottolog groups under Chaldean Neo-Aramaic (chal1275). Corroborating first-hand statements read: Rhétoré 1912 (dialecte de la plaine de Mossoul = Alqosh/Telkepe area, chal1275 proper), Napiorkowska 2015 (Christian Diyana-Zariwaw, listed by Glottolog under chal1275), Khan 2002 snippets (Qaraqosh/Baghdede, Syriac-Catholic town whose dialect Glottolog also files under chal1275), Maclean 1895 (pan-NENA, Urmi-centred, i.e. mostly assy1241 but explicitly covering the 'Plain of Mosul'/Alqosh). All agree on regular penultimate word stress; only Rhétoré 1912 additionally claims final stress for consonant-final words, which the modern descriptions do not support.

new_statements.quote: Word stress is mostly penultimate, as is generally the case in Christian dialects of Iraq; e.g. mašəlxā́na ‘robber’, kəmšāqə́llə ‘he took it’. Non-penultimate stress can be found in specific verbal forms, e.g. mášəlxu ‘rob! (pl)’, kpāθə́xwālə ‘he used to open it’. As a result of this, stress is marginally phonemic: mbā́šəllə ‘cook it!’ mbāšə́llə ‘(that) he may cook it’. In this paper, word stress will only be marked where it is not penultimate.

Chapter 'The Neo-Aramaic Dialect of Telkepe' by Eleanor Coghill runs pp. 235-272 = printed 234-271 (next chapter, Aloni on Zakho, starts pdf 273). extracted text of p. 240 and the page render footer '239') both show sec. 2.2 'Word stress' with the quoted passage word for word: 'Word stress is mostly penultimate, as is generally the case in Christian dialects of Iraq; e.g. mašəlxā́na.. In this paper, word stress will only be marked where it is not penultimate.' The further remarks are also where the compiler placed them: printed p. 248 (pdf 249) 'Alqosh and Qaraqosh have also borrowed the Arabic plural -ā́t, but in those dialects it has lost the stress, in line with t…
new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog (penultimate; Sara 1974 for Mangesh), but for a different dialect of chal1275: Telkepe, spoken by the Chaldean Catholics of Telkepe/Tall Kayf 15 km north of Mosul (Glottolog telk1238 under chal1275), not Mangesh. It adds the exception classes (initial-stress imperatives, -wā- verb forms, final-stressed Arabic -āt plurals, numeral phrases) and states that stress is thereby 'marginally phonemic' in Telkepe, a mild difference from Sara's 'no distinctive function.. completely predictable' for Mangesh; it also confirms penultimate stress for Alqosh and Qaraqosh and for 'Christian dialects of Iraq' generally.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the penultimate syllable by default (as in the Christian NENA dialects of Iraq generally); departures are morphologically conditioned, so stress is only marginally contrastive.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed at the word level. The chapter treats phrase-level stress: words and morphemes often combine into a phrase with a single stress (marked = when the stress is on the second component, ꞊ when on the first; footnote 17 p. 239; Appendix p. 270), and nuclear stress in the intonation phrase is marked with small caps.
new_statements.exceptions: Imperatives take initial stress (mášəlxu ‘rob (pl)!’, p. 239; ‘The Imperative takes initial stress, as in many other NENA dialects’, p. 256); certain verb forms with the past converter, e.g. kpāθə́xwālə ‘he used to open it’ (p. 239), giving minimal pairs like mbā́šəllə ‘cook it!’ vs mbāšə́llə ‘(that) he may cook it’; the borrowed Arabic plural -ā́t keeps final stress in Telkepe (pl primuzā́t), whereas ‘Alqosh and Qaraqosh have also borrowed the Arabic plural -ā́t, but in those dialects it has lost the stress, in line with the native penultimate stress, e.g. Alq. maḥállə ‘town quarter’, pl maḥállat’ (p. 248); numerals used attributively before a noun shift stress to the final syllable (ʾarbé꞊ʾənšə ‘four women’, ʾəšwā́꞊ʾənšə ‘seven women’) and in compound numerals ‘Stress is placed on the final syllable of the unit: ʾarbá-w꞊əsri ‘twenty-four’’ (p. 251); the negator la꞊ takes the stress of the phrase (p. 256).
new_statements.identity_note: Coghill 2018 describes the Telkepe dialect (Chaldean Catholic town of Telkepe/Tall Kayf, southern Mosul Plain; Glottolog telk1238, a dialect of chal1275), not the Mangesh dialect (mang1421) that the catalog record and Sara 1974 describe; both are dialects of Chaldean Neo-Aramaic per Glottolog. McPherson & Ryan 2011 is about Senaya (sena1268, Christian Neo-Aramaic of Sanandaj, Iranian Kurdistan), which is not chal1275 at all.

sources.note: §70 monosyllables bear the accent; §71 polysyllables have the accent on the ultima or penult: on the ultima in words ending in a 'quiescent letter' (consonant), e.g. kthawan 'notre livre', chaklet 'tu prends'; on the penult in words ending in a vowel, e.g. Mara, malpani, taiboutha; proclitic groups (plit-oua-ly) take one accent on the penult of the group; §72 foreign words keep their own accent (ouâli) unless nativized (khadâma).

sources.note: 'In speaking the accent is almost invariably placed on the penultimate, even in foreign words.' Exceptions: vocatives on the first syllable; words with 3pl suffix often oxytone (esp. Urmi); adverbs in -a'it oxytone; some adverbs/particles on the first; 2pl suffix and pl. imperative often antepenultimate; affixes and enclitic verb 'to be' count as part of the word; Sal./Q./Gaw. plurals oxytone after loss of final syllable. Pan-dialectal (Urmi-centred, includes Alqosh 'Al.').

tone.quote: En soureth, la plupart des mots reçoivent un accent tonique sur l’avant derniere syllabe. Certaines formes flechies ou suffixees font exception : grə́ šlawxun [gˈrəʃlawxun] ‘vous avez tire’ ; grə́ šwale [gˈrəʃwaːle] ‘il avait tire’ ; qáša-yle [ˈqaːʃɛi̯le] ‘il est pretre’ ; bgráša-ywatwa [bᵊgˈraːʃɛi̯watwa] ‘tu (fem.) avais ete en train de tirer’… Certains mots d’emprunt peuvent etre accentues sur la derniere syllabe : fərmān [fərˈmaːn] ‘decret’.
tone.translation: In Sureth, most words receive a tonic accent (word stress) on the penultimate syllable. Certain inflected or suffixed forms are exceptions: grə́ šlawxun 'you (pl.) pulled'; grə́ šwale 'he had pulled'; qáša-yle 'he is a priest'; bgráša-ywatwa 'you (f.) had been pulling'... Certain loanwords may be stressed on the last syllable: fərmān 'decree'.
tone.n_tones: None described: prosody section treats word stress only
